items.title: The human evidence is small
items.body:
Plant ecdysteroids are discussed in sports nutrition. The key question is not what a compound is claimed to do, but what controlled human research has measured.

A 2024 review names ecdysterone and this compound as two plant steroids discussed for sport and nutrition. That paper is a review, not a controlled human trial.
items.alt: Open scientific papers and a magnifying glass on linen beside a botanical leaf

items.title: One acute study found no effect
items.body:
A preliminary human study gave multiple acute doses of the compound to 11 apparently healthy males and checked blood IGF-1 and resting metabolic rate before, three hours after, and 24 hours after ingestion.

The authors reported no significant condition, time, or interaction effects. This was an acute study, not a test of long-term muscle growth or performance.

chart.title: What the acute study measured
chart.source: Harris et al., Muscles 2024; acute preliminary study.

items.alt: Running shoes and a stopwatch beside research notes on a track-side bench
items.evidence_label: Human study · Harris et al., Muscles 2024

items.title: IGF-1 did not reach significance
items.body:
The same study explored serum IGF-1, a marker sometimes used in discussions of muscle biology. The reported analyses did not find a statistically significant effect.

A non-significant rise is not proof of an anabolic benefit. The study also did not measure added muscle over a training block.
items.alt: A timer, an open notebook, a pen, and a small capsule on a linen table
items.evidence_label: Human study · IGF-1 result reported without significance

items.title: Related compounds differ
items.body:
Some human discussion centers on ecdysterone, a related ecdysteroid, rather than the compound in this guide. Related compounds can inform a research question, but they are not interchangeable evidence.

Ingredient identity matters. A result for ecdysterone is not a result for the other compound unless a trial tested that compound.

chart.title: Read the compound name carefully
chart.source: Todorova et al., Nutrients 2024; review of ecdysteroid compounds.

items.alt: Barbell plate, chalk, and a muscle-fiber sketch on a paper study board

items.title: Animal data stays preclinical
items.body:
Plant ecdysteroid research also includes laboratory and animal models. Those experiments can suggest mechanisms worth testing, but they do not establish an effect in lifters.

The 2025 stress-resilience paper cited here studied Caenorhabditis elegans, not people. It did not test a commercial formula, human muscle growth, or training performance.
items.evidence: Animal model, International Journal of Molecular Sciences 2025
items.alt: Laboratory glassware and abstract plant tissue on a softly lit research bench

items.title: The product has no matching trial
items.body:
The acute study tested the compound. It did not test a finished commercial formula. A research intervention and a product label are not automatically the same thing.

We found no published human trial of a commercial formula in the sources reviewed for this page. That is an evidence gap, not evidence of either benefit or harm.
items.evidence: Evidence gap, exact-product trial not found in reviewed sources
items.alt: Blank grid paper, reading glasses, and a cup on a linen table
items.evidence_label: Evidence gap · exact-product trial not found

items.title: Consistency is still untested
items.body:
The available human study looked at short-term measurements after ingestion. It did not test a repeated training routine, strength progression, recovery across sessions, or long-term safety.

For lifters, that missing time horizon is important. Do not turn a short observation into a promise about months of training.
items.alt: A gym bag, towel, dumbbells, and a water glass on a morning bench
items.evidence_label: Study limitation · no long-term training outcome

bridge.title: Convenience is part of consistency
bridge.body:
Research questions become practical only when a routine is easy to inspect and repeat. The evidence here does not promise a training result.
